one_liner: Rust static xor/binary-fuse filters: about 9 bits/key at 0.4% FPP versus about 11.5 for an optimal Bloom.
what_it_does: xorf is an approximate-membership filter crate for a fixed set of u64 keys, with no false negatives. You build it once from a slice, Vec or ExactSizeIterator of distinct u64 hashes (`BinaryFuse8::try_from(&keys)`) and query it with `contains(&u64)`; the built filter cannot be changed (no inserts, deletes or merges). Families: BinaryFuse8/16/32 (recommended, fallible build), Xor8/16/32 (infallible `From`) and the deprecated Fuse8/16/32. There is also a `HashProxy` for arbitrary `Hash` key types, Serde support, and zero-copy `*Ref` views over mmap'd buffers through `DmaSerializable`/`FilterRef`.
how_it_is_fast: Each key maps to three fingerprint slots: construction peels a random 3-uniform hypergraph so that fingerprint(key) = F[h0] ^ F[h1] ^ F[h2], and a query is one MurmurHash3 finalizer mix plus three array reads, with no SIMD. Binary fuse filters (Graf & Lemire, arXiv:2201.01174) put the three slots in adjacent power-of-two segments (a binary-partitioned fuse graph), so the array needs about 1.125n slots instead of the xor filter's 1.23n + 32. Fingerprint width alone sets the FPP (about 2^-8, 2^-16 or 2^-32) at about 9, 18 or 36 bits/key, where a Bloom filter needs about 1.44·log2(1/ε) bits/key. The code is a port of Go FastFilter/xorfilter and uses only the 3-wise variant.
when_to_use: Static or rebuild-occasionally sets that are queried far more often than built, such as SST/segment filters, blocklists, dedup pre-checks and 'is this key on disk' guards, where filter RAM is what you are trying to cut.
You already have 64-bit hashes, or can hash keys yourself, and a fixed FPP of about 0.39% (8-bit), about 0.0015% (16-bit) or effectively zero (32-bit) suits you.
Rust services or embedded/no_std targets with an allocator. CI checks thumbv7em-none-eabi with default features off.
Filters persisted to disk and loaded without copying: `BinaryFuse*Ref::from_dma` borrows the fingerprint bytes from an mmap'd buffer and copies only a 20-byte descriptor.
Sets of about a million keys or more. The paper measures the 3-wise layout reaching 9 bits/key there, while below about 20k keys the xor filter can be as small or smaller.
when_not_to_use: You need inserts, deletes or counting. Every filter is rebuilt from the full key set; use a cuckoo or quotient filter instead.

You want to tune FPP against space continuously, the way Bloom parameters allow. Only 8, 16 and 32-bit fingerprints exist, and the maintainer says in issues #61 and #69 that space per item cannot be reduced.

Query latency on huge filters is the goal. Each lookup touches three random cache lines. A user in issue #84 measured about 280 M lookups/s at 1M keys falling to about 51 M/s at 99M keys, and in the binary fuse paper an AVX2 blocked Bloom filter queried faster than any xor-family filter.

Building very large sets under a memory cap. From reading the code, BinaryFuse construction allocates about 13 bytes per slot plus 9 bytes per key of scratch (about 24 B/key) on top of your u64 key array, for a result of about 1.1 B/key.
You need the smallest possible static filter. xorf has no 4-wise binary fuse (8.6 bits/key in the paper), and Ribbon filters (BuRR, RocksDB) get closer to the lower bound.

integration.dependencies: libm (via the default `binary-fuse` feature) and rand (via the default `uniform-random` feature, which needs std). Optional: serde plus serde_bytes. The published 0.13.0 also has an optional `bincode` 2.0.0-rc.3 dependency, which is flagged unmaintained (RUSTSEC-2025-0141, issue #98). Unreleased master (0.14.0) removes it and keeps `bincode` only as an alias for `serde`.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.85 on master (edition 2024, MSRV job in CI). The published 0.13.0 is edition 2021 and declares no rust-version, so its MSRV is not documented.
integration.platforms: Any Rust target with `alloc`. The code is portable and has no arch-specific intrinsics. no_std builds are CI-checked on thumbv7em-none-eabi without default features.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Built filters are immutable, `contains` takes &self, and the fields are plain owned data (Descriptor plus Box<[uN]>), so the auto traits make them Send + Sync and safe to share read-only.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces a Bloom filter only for static sets. You must pre-hash keys to distinct u64s (or use HashProxy), build all at once, accept a fixed FPP per fingerprint width, and handle a fallible build for BinaryFuse. There are no add, union or clear operations.

gotchas: Keys must be distinct. Debug builds check this with a BTreeSet and panic; in release, BinaryFuse drops exact duplicate hashes, but the Xor family's unbounded retry loop never terminates on duplicates (issue #25). BinaryFuse gives up after 1,000 deterministic seeds with Err("Failed to construct binary fuse filter."), and before 0.13.0 about 1 in 60k distinct key sets just past a segment-length step (n ≈ 11.5k) could never build (PR #100).

`HashProxy` requires `From<Vec<u64>>`, which BinaryFuse types do not implement (they only have TryFrom), so the recommended filters cannot be wrapped. Issue #72 is closed, but the code still lacks the impl. Hash keys yourself or wrap Xor8 instead.

Filter bytes are not reproducible by default. The `uniform-random` feature fills unused slots from the thread RNG (issue #77); disable default features for byte-identical output. DMA fingerprints for the 16/32-bit types are raw native-endian memory, although the descriptor is little-endian, and `from_dma` panics on misaligned buffers (it uses unsafe `from_raw_parts` after assert checks).

The README on master says `xorf = "0.14"`, but crates.io's newest version is 0.13.0, so that line does not resolve yet. BinaryFuse index arithmetic is u32, so one filter addresses at most 2^32 slots (about 3.8B keys); this limit is not documented.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick xorf when you are in Rust and want the xor_singleheader/xorfilter algorithms natively, with no_std support and zero-copy mmap loading; use those C/Go originals in their own languages. Choose BuRR or RocksDB Ribbon instead when the last few percent of space matter more than query speed (the binary fuse paper measured ribbon queries slower), and a cuckoo filter or CQF when the set must accept inserts or deletes.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing in this crate measures a Bloom filter: its doc tests only assert BinaryFuse8 stays under 9.1 bits/key with under 0.406% false positives on 1M random u64 keys, and its Criterion benches time only xorf's own filters (the lookup bench repeats one hot key). The Bloom comparison (binary fuse within 13% of the storage lower bound vs 44% for Bloom, i.e. about 9 vs about 11.5 bits/key at 2^-8) comes from the binary fuse paper (JEA 2022), which benchmarks the authors' C++ code (GCC 10 -O3 -march=native, Intel i7-6700 Skylake), not this Rust port; the 9-bit figure carries over by construction, but speed does not.
status_note: Actively maintained and MIT-licensed, with about 6.7M crates.io downloads: 0.13.0 shipped on 2026-08-21 with the segment-boundary construction fix, and master already carries an unreleased 0.14.0 (edition 2024, MSRV 1.85, native bincode support removed).
